processing: Fresh vine leaf is processed mostly on automated factory lines today, with traditional Tujia methods still kept alive in workshops. The white bloom it is known for forms in processing as flavonoids such as dihydromyricetin crystallise.
harvest_season: Local harvest calendars are little recorded; as with vine tea generally, the heaviest growth comes in early summer, followed by autumn.
appearance_dry: Twisted leaf and stem under an obvious white frost.
appearance_liquor: Clear light yellow-green, as is usual for frosted vine tea.
appearance_wet: Slim, toothed leaves on thin stems, as is usual for vine tea.
taste_profile: As with other vine teas, a light bitterness and grassy note followed by a strong lasting sweetness.

brewing.notes: Brew as you would a green tea. The frost dissolves into the cup, so do not rinse it away, and do not mistake it for mould.

vintage_note: Sold as recent production rather than by year, usually with a place of origin and a certification on the pack. No aged market is established. Check for the geographical indication mark if you want the real Yongding product.
description:
Mei cha is the Zhangjiajie trade name for vine tea, made from Nekemias grossedentata. It is the same species as teng cha, but mei cha names the protected local product. Its home is Yongding District, above all Luotaping Township, where Changshou Village calls itself the first mei cha village in China.

The vine grows on misty slopes roughly between 400 and 1,500 metres, with the core zone at 800 to 1,500, on loose acid sandstone soils. Most leaf now goes from farmers to factories, where automated lines handle it. A white frost forms during processing as flavonoids crystallise, and that frost is not mould.

In the cup it should behave like other vine teas: a slight bitterness and a grassy edge, then a long sweetness. Treat it as a green tea with hot water and moderate steeps, and try a few rounds, as the sweetness builds.

Look for the geographical indication mark and a named Yongding origin, since the plant grows widely and the word mei cha travels well beyond Zhangjiajie. Local promotion leans on health claims about the high flavonoid content, and they should not be your reason to buy.
history:
Tujia people are reported to have drunk it for generations, but dated detail for this local name is scarce; the wider history of vine tea and its legends belongs to teng cha.

What is clear is its recent rise into an organised industry. It holds a national geographical indication certification mark, with dozens of firms approved to use it, and Yongding has set local planting and processing standards and traceability schemes. Workshops at a mei cha town still show the old Tujia handwork beside modern lines.
